title: The Long-Haired Star: Spring 1066
subtitle: Halley's Comet over Eurasia in the year of Stamford Bridge and Hastings, March–June 1066
intro: In the spring of 1066 the comet now named after Edmond Halley swung around the Sun (perihelion fell around 20–23 March) and passed unusually close to the Earth in late April, at roughly a tenth of the Earth–Sun distance. For about two months it was one of the most conspicuous objects in the sky from Ireland to Japan. It rose first as a dawn object in the east, then vanished into the Sun's glare. Around 24 April it reappeared in the evening sky in the north-west with a long tail, and it faded through May into early June.

No one who saw it kept a diary in the modern sense. The honest record is made of annals, chronicles, an official astronomical register and one embroidered strip of linen, and the form tags say so. Some of it is close to contemporary: the Chinese bureau's daily positions, the English chronicles kept at Abingdon and Worcester, William of Jumièges writing in Normandy within a few years. Much of it was written down later: Zonaras and Matthew of Edessa in the twelfth century, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn al-Athir in the late twelfth and early thirteenth, the Goryeosa in 1451, the Annals of the Four Masters in the 1630s. Each eye carries a note on when its words were set down.

The heart of the chapter is the week of 24 April. The Chinese astronomers at Kaifeng logged the comet's return as a white vapour, then measured a tail more than ten degrees long. The English scribes wrote that it was first seen on the eve of the Greater Litany and shone for seven nights. The Irish annals put it on the Tuesday after Low Sunday, and a Norman monk saw a three-forked tail in the north-west. Japanese courtiers saw it in the west at dusk. In each place it was read through local expectations. To the Song bureau it was a broom star to be measured against the lunar lodges. The Rus' chronicler saw blood in its rays. To an old monk at Malmesbury it was a scourge to England.

On the ground, the year was crowded. Edward the Confessor died on 5 January and Harold Godwinson was crowned the next day. Tostig raided the English coast soon after the comet's week. Harald Hardrada and Tostig fell at Stamford Bridge on 25 September. William of Normandy landed at Pevensey three days later, won at Hastings on 14 October and was crowned on Christmas Day. Later writers bent the comet towards these events. The Bayeux Tapestry sets it just after Harold's coronation, months before it actually appeared. One Norman poem moves it to the autumn landing. These rearrangements are set out here as positions, beside the dated sky.

The eastern records do something the western ones do not. They give lodge-by-lodge positions and dates that modern astronomers have used to check the comet's orbit, and Kevin Yau's reconstruction suggests that the April positions imply a perihelion two or three days later than the tabulated date. The same sky that frightened kings has become data.
calendar_note: date_iso uses the proleptic Julian calendar, as historians of 1066 cite it (add six days for the Gregorian equivalent). English dates are given in the Roman reckoning: the eighth day before the Kalends of May (VIII Kal. Mai.) is 24 April, the eve of the Greater Litany (25 April, St Mark's day). Easter fell on 16 April 1066, so Low Sunday ('Little Easter') was 23 April and the Irish 'Tuesday after Little Easter' (VII Kal. Mai.) is 25 April. Song Chinese dates are reign years of Zhiping (Zhiping 3 = 1066) with sexagenary day names. The days given here (3 April = gengshen, 24 April = xinsi, 25 April = renwu, 26 April = guiwei, 7 June = yichou) are computed from the Julian Day count; the lunar month numbers are not stated because they were not checked against a calendar table. Korean dates are in the 20th year of King Munjong of Goryeo and Japanese dates in the 2nd year of Jiryaku. Hijri dates are converted with the tabular calendar and may be off by a day or two: 1 Muharram 458 ≈ 3 December 1065, 10 Jumada I 458 ≈ 9 April 1066, mid-Jumada II ≈ 14 May, mid-Rajab ≈ 13 June. The Armenian year 515 began on 5 March 1066. The Byzantine year AM 6574 ran from 1 September 1065 to 31 August 1066. The Rus' Primary Chronicle places its blood-rayed star under 6573, a year that should end in February 1066. Its identification with Halley's Comet is usual, but it implies a slip in the chronicle's dating.

eyes.name: Anonymous scribes of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (versions C and D)
eyes.role: Monastic annalists keeping the vernacular year-by-year chronicle; C usually located at Abingdon, D associated with Worcester and York circles
eyes.where: Abingdon Abbey (C), with D kept in the Worcester diocese
eyes.vantage_label: English monks recording the year as it came
eyes.authenticity: Versions C (British Library, Cotton Tiberius B i) and D (Cotton Tiberius B iv) both carry the comet under 1066 in closely similar words; the Peterborough version E does not record it. The 1066 annals were written up within months to a few years of the events. Quoted wording here follows Ingram's 1823 English translation as reprinted by Project Gutenberg.
eyes.bio: The Chronicle is the only English source that registers the comet in the same breath as the year's politics: Harold at Westminster at Easter, the star, then Tostig's raid. Its scribes give the Roman calendar date and the length of the bright spell, and they say plainly that people disagreed about what to call it.

sources.title: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, tr. J. Ingram (1823), Project Gutenberg
Mardon, Mardon & Williams, The Eleven Observations of Comets ... Recorded in the Anglo Saxon Chronicle (LPI, 1992)

eyes.name: Eilmer (Æthelmær) of Malmesbury
eyes.role: Elderly Benedictine monk of Malmesbury Abbey, remembered as a learned man and for an earlier attempt to fly from the abbey tower with wings
eyes.vantage_label: an old monk who remembered an earlier comet
eyes.form: reported speech in a later chronicle (written c. 1125)
eyes.authenticity: Eilmer left no writing. His reaction survives only in William of Malmesbury's Gesta Regum Anglorum (c. 1125), written about sixty years later by a monk of the same house who may have heard it from older brethren. William's report that Eilmer had seen a comet as a boy is often linked to the 989 return of the same comet. That interpretation has recently been promoted as a claim that Eilmer recognised the comet's return, and it remains a modern reading.
eyes.bio: Eilmer is the best-known English witness, though he is known only through a later writer. William of Malmesbury has him crying out at the comet that it would bring tears to many mothers and ruin to England, and recalling a comet he had seen long before.

sources.title: Universe Today, The monk who recognised Halley's comet first
Lewis & Portegies Zwart, The significance of Halley's Comet in the Bayeux Tapestry (arXiv, 2025)

eyes.name: William of Jumièges
eyes.role: Monk of the abbey of Jumièges on the lower Seine, author of the Deeds of the Dukes of the Normans
eyes.vantage_label: a Norman monk across the Channel
eyes.authenticity: The Gesta was compiled in the 1050s–60s and extended after 1067 to cover the Conquest; it was later reworked by Orderic Vitalis and Robert of Torigni, so the original layer must be distinguished from interpolations. His comet passage is the nearest Norman record in time.
eyes.bio: William of Jumièges gives the only near-contemporary Norman description of the comet's look: a star in the north-west with a three-forked tail stretching far into the southern sky, visible about fifteen days. He reports only that many people said it meant a change in some kingdom, without tying it openly to Harold.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Romana: Stella (Bayeux Tapestry and William of Jumièges)
Lewis & Portegies Zwart (arXiv PDF)

eyes.name: William of Poitiers
eyes.role: Former knight turned priest; chaplain to Duke William and archdeacon of Lisieux
eyes.where: Ducal court in Normandy; archdeaconry of Lisieux
eyes.authenticity: The Gesta Guillelmi survives incomplete (the only manuscript, a Cotton manuscript, was lost in the 1731 fire, and the text depends on Duchesne's 1619 edition). Written to justify William's claim, it is well informed on the ducal side and openly partisan.
eyes.bio: Poitiers knew the duke's household and many who fought at Hastings, though he was probably not in the battle himself. He treats the comet as a sign aimed at Harold: a star feared by kings that blazed soon after the usurper's coronation and foretold his fall.

sources.title: William of Poitiers (overview)
Lewis & Portegies Zwart (arXiv PDF)

eyes.name: Designer and embroiderers of the Bayeux Tapestry
eyes.role: Anonymous designer (probably working in Canterbury) and needleworkers, likely commissioned for Bishop Odo of Bayeux, William's half-brother
eyes.where: Probably Canterbury; displayed at Bayeux Cathedral
eyes.authenticity: The embroidery survives at Bayeux, about 70 m long. It is usually dated c. 1070–77 and often linked to the consecration of Bayeux Cathedral in 1077. The comet scene is original, though parts of the hanging were restored in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.
eyes.bio: The Tapestry gives the most famous image of the comet: a flaming star with a streaming tail over a group of pointing men, labelled ISTI MIRANT STELLA ('these men marvel at the star'). Next to it a messenger reports to the newly crowned Harold, and ghostly ships in the lower border hint at invasion. The scene places the comet just after the January coronation, although it appeared in April.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Romana: Stella
Lewis & Portegies Zwart, The significance of Halley's Comet in the Bayeux Tapestry

eyes.name: Astronomers of the Song Astronomical Bureau
eyes.role: Court observers at the Northern Song capital whose daily reports fed the official astronomical record
eyes.side: Northern Song China (Emperor Yingzong, Zhiping era)
eyes.form: official astronomical record (preserved in the Song shi, compiled 1343–45)
eyes.authenticity: The bureau's reports survive in two places in the Song shi, the astronomical treatise and the imperial annals. The two are close but not identical; the annals' 'morning' note for 24 April conflicts with the comet's position and is judged an error by modern analysts. The northern Liao dynasty's history independently records a broom star in the west on 24 April.
eyes.bio: No other observer comes close to the Song bureau's precision. Its astronomers dated the first dawn sighting, tracked the comet through the lunar lodges from Yingshi to Mao, Bi and Zhang, measured the tail's length and width, and reported a total of 67 days. Modern astronomers have used these figures to refine the comet's orbit.

sources.title: K. K. C. Yau, Durham PhD thesis (Far Eastern records of Halley's Comet, ch. 3)
Historical comet observations in China

eyes.name: Astronomical officials of the Goryeo court
eyes.form: official astronomical record (preserved in the Goryeosa, compiled 1451)
eyes.authenticity: Preserved in the astronomical treatise of the Goryeosa, compiled in the early Joseon period from Goryeo court records. Its date (19 April) and direction (north-west) differ from the Chinese and Japanese accounts, and modern analysts treat it with some caution.
eyes.bio: The Korean entry is brief. It records a star in the north-west as large as the Moon, which then turned into a 'comet' (huibo, a bushy star). Its oddities are useful: they show how far court records could drift from one another.

sources.title: K. K. C. Yau, Durham PhD thesis

eyes.name: Japanese court observers and diarists (Heian period)
eyes.role: Observers of the onmyōryō (Bureau of Divination) and court record-keepers under Emperor Go-Reizei
eyes.form: court records and diary notices (compiled in Kanda Shigeru, Nihon tenmon shiryō, 1935)
eyes.authenticity: The Japanese notices come from several court sources gathered in Kanda's compendium; Yau's analysis cites a composite record and a notice he labels Sankaiki. Which original diary or chronicle stands behind each line was not checked here.
eyes.bio: The Japanese record agrees with the Chinese on the first morning. A broom star about seven degrees long was seen in the east on 3 April, and the comet was seen again in the west at dusk on 27 April. A second notice says it was seen in the east for about twenty days, disappeared, and was later seen in the west. That is how the dawn-to-dusk switch looked from Kyoto.

sources.title: K. K. C. Yau, Durham PhD thesis

eyes.name: John Zonaras
eyes.role: Former high official of the Byzantine court turned monk, author of the Epitome of Histories
eyes.where: Constantinople (the comet's Byzantine witnesses); Zonaras wrote later in exile on an island in the Sea of Marmara
eyes.authenticity: Zonaras compiled his Epitome decades after 1066 from earlier Byzantine histories; his comet notice is therefore secondhand, though placed securely in the reign of Constantine X Doukas (1059–1067).
eyes.bio: Zonaras gives the comet's Byzantine description: as bright as the full moon and at first without a tail, then sprouting a tail while its head seemed to shrink. He sets it in the reign of Constantine X Doukas, who died in May 1067, a court where omens were read with political anxiety.

sources.title: G. F. Chambers, The Story of the Comets (1909), p. 118 (Wikisource mirror)
Prosopography of the Byzantine World: Konstantinos X Doukas

eyes.name: Abu'l-Faraj ibn al-Jawzi
eyes.role: Hanbali jurist and preacher of Baghdad, author of the annalistic history al-Muntazam
eyes.authenticity: Al-Muntazam was compiled a century after 1066 from Baghdad registers and earlier annals. The date here (10 Jumada I) comes from a modern English quotation in Aramco World (1986), which does not state the Hijri year. It is assigned to 458 AH because the description and the converted date fit the comet.
eyes.bio: Ibn al-Jawzi's Baghdad entry captures the whole apparition: first a large comet whose long tail stretched up to the zenith, then the comet reappearing at sunset with its tail thrown southwards for about ten days. The two phases match the Chinese record of a dawn object followed by an evening one.

sources.title: Aramco World (Jan/Feb 1986), The Long-Haired Star

eyes.name: Ali 'Izz al-Din ibn al-Athir
eyes.role: Historian of Mosul, author of the universal chronicle al-Kamil fi'l-ta'rikh
eyes.side: Islamic Near East (Zangid Mosul, writing of Seljuk-era events)
eyes.where: Mosul (where he wrote); the sighting reported from Iraq
eyes.authenticity: Al-Kamil was written some 150 years later and draws on earlier annals, Ibn al-Jawzi's among them. As quoted in Aramco World, his notice for 458 AH puts the comet in mid-Jumada II (about mid-May 1066), seen before dawn. In mid-May the comet was an evening object, so the month or the timing is probably garbled.
eyes.bio: Ibn al-Athir supplies a measurement in the Arab manner: a white comet that looked about ten cubits long and one cubit wide. He says it lasted until mid-Rajab, about mid-June, which agrees with the Chinese end-date. His dawn timing and month are a puzzle and are shown in the ledger as disputed.

sources.title: Aramco World (Jan/Feb 1986), The Long-Haired Star

eyes.name: Matthew of Edessa
eyes.role: Armenian monk and abbot in Edessa, author of a chronicle of the years 952–1136
eyes.authenticity: Matthew compiled his chronicle in the early twelfth century from older Armenian accounts and oral tradition; his early chronology is often loose. The comet appears under the Armenian Era year 515 (A.D. 1066–67), in Robert Bedrosian's translation.
eyes.bio: Matthew's account is short but notes the comet's two phases clearly. It appeared in the east and moved westward, was visible for a month and vanished, then reappeared many days later in the west, and people said it was the same comet. He places it just before an account of invaders ruining Armenian lands, which implies it was an omen.

sources.title: Chronicle of Matthew of Edessa, tr. R. Bedrosian (2017), PDF

eyes.name: Compiler of the Rus' Primary Chronicle (Povest' vremennykh let)
eyes.life: compiled c. 1110s (traditionally attributed to Nestor of the Kyiv Caves Monastery)
eyes.role: Monk-chronicler of Kyiv drawing on earlier annals
eyes.authenticity: The Primary Chronicle survives in the Laurentian (1377) and Hypatian (c. 1425) codices. The star appears under 6573, alongside a solar sign and a deformed infant hauled from the Setoml river. The compiler says he examined the infant himself. The identification of the star with Halley's Comet is usual but implies a dating slip.
eyes.bio: The Kyiv chronicler saw a very large star in the west with blood-red rays, rising in the evening after sunset and lasting seven days. He read it as bloodshed to come: feuds among princes and pagan raids on the Rus' land. His evening star in the west agrees with the comet's late-April appearance seen elsewhere.

sources.title: Povist' mynulykh lit, Ukrainian text, page 25 (osvita.ua)

eyes.name: Irish annalists (Annals of Ulster; Annals of the Four Masters)
eyes.life: fl. 11th century (source annals); Four Masters compiled 1632–36
eyes.role: Monastic annalists whose year-entries were later compiled by Mícheál Ó Cléirigh and colleagues in Donegal
eyes.where: Ireland (monastic annal centres; observing place not stated)
eyes.vantage_label: the western edge of the comet's audience
eyes.form: annals (Annals of Ulster near-contemporary; Four Masters compiled later)
eyes.authenticity: The Annals of Ulster entry for 1066 survives but does not mention the star. The Four Masters (1630s) record it under M1066, drawing on older Irish annals now partly lost. Another Irish annal tradition, quoted without citation online, describes a strange, enormous hairy star dated VIII Kal. Mai. (24 April), but its source annal was not identified here.
eyes.bio: The Irish entry is terse but exactly dated. A star appeared on the seventh of the Kalends of May, on the Tuesday after Little Easter, which is 25 April 1066. That is the day after the English 'eve of the Litany', so the two neighbouring records fall one night apart. The Annals of Ulster's own 1066 entry records a nut harvest heavy enough to choke the rivers.

sources.title: Annals of the Four Masters, M1066 (CELT)
Annals of Ulster, U1066 (CELT)

entries.date_display: Thursday 5 January 1066 (Julian), the eve of Twelfth Day
entries.headline: King Edward dies on the eve of Twelfth Day
entries.digest: The Chronicle records that Edward died on the eve of the Epiphany, soon after the consecration of his new abbey church at Westminster. The annal treats the death as the end of a long, peaceful reign and does not mention any sign in the sky. The comet was still almost three months away.
entries.source_note: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle s.a. 1065 (C/D), Ingram tr., Project Gutenberg

entries.headline: Edward buried, Harold hallowed king the same day
entries.digest: Edward was buried at Westminster on Twelfth Day, and the Chronicle states that Earl Harold was hallowed king. English versions present him as Edward's chosen successor. The speed of the coronation, within a day of the funeral, later became central to Norman arguments.
entries.source_note: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle s.a. 1065/1066, Ingram tr. with Giles collation

entries.headline: A chaplain brands the coronation a perjurer's seizure
entries.digest: William of Poitiers describes Harold taking the throne on the very day of the funeral as a usurpation by a man who had sworn an oath to Duke William. In his account an archbishop of doubtful standing performed the consecration. The scene sets up the duke's invasion as a just war.
entries.source_note: Gesta Guillelmi, as summarised in Lewis & Portegies Zwart 2025 and standard overviews; edition not checked directly

entries.headline: Edward's deathbed, funeral and Harold enthroned in linen
entries.digest: The Tapestry shows Edward's body carried to Westminster and his deathbed scene, then Harold enthroned holding orb and sceptre with Archbishop Stigand beside him. Crowds acclaim him. The next scene, without any break, is the comet.
entries.source_note: Bayeux Tapestry scenes 26–31; Lewis & Portegies Zwart 2025

entries.date_display: 3 February 6574 (1066), as given in the Primary Chronicle
entries.headline: Prince Rostislav poisoned by a Greek official
entries.digest: Under 6574 the Kyiv chronicle tells how Rostislav, prince of Tmutarakan on the Black Sea straits, was poisoned at a feast by a Byzantine official from Chersonesos, who was then stoned by the townspeople. The incident is a reminder that Rus' politics and Byzantine politics overlapped. The chronicler had already placed his blood-rayed star in the previous year's entry.
entries.source_note: Primary Chronicle s.a. 6574; date recalled from standard editions, not fetched

entries.headline: Broom star at dawn in Yingshi, seven degrees long
entries.digest: Before dawn the Song astronomers logged a broom star (huixing) in the lunar lodge Yingshi, its tail about seven degrees long and pointing south-west towards the lodge Wei. The annals give the same day and place, 'in the morning'. This is the earliest dated sighting of the apparition anywhere.
entries.source_note: Song shi, astronomical treatise and annals, as tabulated in Yau, Durham thesis ch. 3 (return of AD 1066)

entries.date_display: Jiryaku 2, morning of the day corresponding to 3 April 1066
entries.headline: Kyoto sees the same broom star in the east
entries.digest: On the same morning, the Japanese court record notes a broom star in the east about seven degrees long. Kyoto is about two hours of longitude east of Kaifeng, so the Japanese observers would have seen it in the pre-dawn sky before the Chinese. The two courts did not know of each other's records.
entries.source_note: Composite Japanese record (Kanda) as tabulated in Yau, ch. 3

entries.headline: Twenty days in the east, then gone, then in the west
entries.digest: A second Japanese notice, which Yau labels Sankaiki, covers the dawn phase as a single stretch. The broom star was seen in the east, after about twenty days it was no longer seen, and it was later seen in the west. The notice records the comet's passage behind the Sun without explaining it.
entries.source_note: Yau, ch. 3; original source attribution not checked

entries.date_display: 10 Jumada I [458 AH] (≈ 9 April 1066, tabular conversion)
entries.headline: A great comet with its tail at the zenith
entries.digest: The Baghdad annal records a large comet whose long tail stretched up to the zenith. The tail is described as pointing east, which is probably the compiler's or the translator's simplification. The date falls a week after the first Chinese and Japanese sightings, in the comet's dawn phase.
entries.source_note: al-Muntazam as quoted in Aramco World 1986; Hijri year inferred

entries.headline: Harold keeps Easter at Westminster
entries.digest: The Chronicle notes that Harold came from York to Westminster for the Easter after Edward's death, and dates Easter to the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May. The comet had already been seen at dawn in Asia, but no English writer mentions it yet. The next lines of the annal bring the star.
entries.source_note: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle s.a. 1066, Ingram tr.

entries.headline: A star as large as the Moon becomes a comet
entries.digest: The Goryeo record says a star appeared in the north-west as large as the Moon and then changed into a bushy comet. The date falls inside the few days when the comet was lost in the Sun's glare elsewhere, and the north-west direction fits the evening reappearance a few days later. Modern analysts note the mismatch and leave it unresolved.
entries.source_note: Goryeosa astronomical treatise, as given in Yau, ch. 3

entries.headline: A white vapour returns; the comet in Mao, 'like Venus'
entries.digest: The treatise records a white vapour, which modern readers identify as the comet's tail as it re-emerged. The annals place the comet in the lodge Mao (the Pleiades), as bright as Venus and fifteen degrees long, though they wrongly call it a morning sighting. On the same day the Liao court in the north recorded a broom star in the west.
entries.source_note: Song shi treatise and annals; Liao shi annals; all as given in Yau, ch. 3

entries.date_display: VIII Kal. Mai., the eve of the Greater Litany (Monday 24 April 1066)
entries.headline: Over all England, a sign no one had seen before
entries.digest: The C and D chroniclers write that a sign was seen throughout England such as no one had seen before. Some said it was a comet, which others call the long-haired star. It first appeared on the eve of the Greater Litany and shone for the whole week. The entry is one of only a few in the Chronicle to give a comet a calendar date.
entries.source_note: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle s.a. 1066 (C, D), Ingram tr., Project Gutenberg

entries.headline: Tail over ten degrees long and three wide
entries.digest: The bureau measured the comet's spread for the first time: more than ten degrees long and more than three degrees wide. The annals have it emerging in the lodge Bi (the Hyades). The comet was then near its closest approach to the Earth, and its apparent motion from night to night was fast.
entries.source_note: Yau, ch. 3

entries.date_display: VII Kal. Mai., Tuesday after Little Easter (25 April 1066)
entries.headline: A star on the Tuesday after Little Easter
entries.digest: The Irish annal records only that a star appeared, and dates it by both the Roman calendar and the Easter cycle. Both reckonings agree on 25 April, one night after the English date. The entry has no omen attached, which is unusual among the western records.
entries.source_note: Annals of the Four Masters M1066.11 (CELT T100005B)

entries.headline: The tail stretches to fifteen degrees
entries.digest: Two nights after the reappearance, the treatise gives the tail as fifteen degrees long. Yau argues that this lengthening reflects the comet's closeness to the Earth around 23 April. Fitting the Mao and Bi positions puts perihelion about 23.5 March, slightly later than the computed 20.9 March.
entries.source_note: Yau, ch. 3

entries.date_display: late April 1066 (c. 26 April as commonly given)
entries.headline: A three-forked tail across the southern sky
entries.digest: William of Jumièges describes a star in the north-west whose three-forked tail stretched far into the southern sky, visible for about fifteen days. He reports, without committing himself, that many people took it to signal a change in some kingdom. His text gives no day; the 26 April date often attached to the Norman sighting comes from modern commentary.
entries.source_note: Gesta Normannorum Ducum, as summarised by Encyclopaedia Romana and Lewis & Portegies Zwart 2025

entries.date_display: Jiryaku 2, evening of the day corresponding to 27 April 1066 (hour of the cock, c. 5–7 p.m.)
entries.headline: Now in the west at dusk
entries.digest: The Japanese court record places the comet in the west during the evening double-hour. Three weeks earlier it had been in the east before dawn. The two notices, read together, show the dawn and dusk phases of the same comet.
entries.source_note: Composite Japanese record (Kanda) as given in Yau, ch. 3

entries.headline: An old monk addresses the star as a scourge
entries.digest: According to William of Malmesbury, the aged Eilmer spoke to the comet directly when he saw it. He said it had come to bring tears to many mothers and that he had seen it long ago, and he foresaw the downfall of England. The speech was written down about sixty years later and is reported, not recorded.
entries.source_note: William of Malmesbury, Gesta Regum Anglorum II.225, as summarised in Lewis & Portegies Zwart 2025 and press reports

entries.date_display: spring 1066 (entered under AM 6573 in the Primary Chronicle)
entries.headline: A great star with bloody rays, seven evenings
entries.digest: The chronicler records a sign in the west: a very large star with blood-red rays that rose in the evening after sunset and remained seven days. He interprets it at once as bloodshed to come, with feuds among the princes and pagan raids on the land. In the same entry he lists other ominous signs, including a dimmed sun and a deformed infant.
entries.source_note: Primary Chronicle s.a. 6573, Ukrainian text at osvita.ua

entries.date_display: spring 1066 (AM 6574, reign of Constantine X Doukas; told in the 12th century)
entries.headline: Bright as the full moon, then a tail
entries.digest: Zonaras reports that in Constantine Doukas's reign a comet appeared, at first as bright as the full moon and without a tail. Later it grew a tail and its head seemed to shrink. He sets it among the signs of a troubled reign rather than giving a day.
entries.source_note: Zonaras, Epitome XVIII, as summarised in Chambers, The Story of the Comets (1909), p. 118

entries.headline: East for a month, then the same star in the west
entries.digest: Matthew records a comet that appeared in the east and moved westward, stayed a month and vanished. Many days later it appeared again in the west, and people said it was the same comet. He places it just before an account of invaders ravaging Armenian lands, which implies it was an omen.
entries.source_note: Chronicle of Matthew of Edessa, Part 2, AE 515, tr. Bedrosian

entries.headline: ISTI MIRANT STELLA: men point at the sky
entries.digest: A group of men point upward at a star with a flaming, streaming tail, labelled 'these men marvel at the star'. Beside them a messenger brings news to Harold on his throne. Below, in the border, empty ships are outlined. The scene compresses January and April into one moment, so the comet appears to answer Harold's coronation.
entries.source_note: Bayeux Tapestry scene 32–33; Encyclopaedia Romana; Lewis & Portegies Zwart 2025

entries.headline: A star feared by kings marks Harold's doom
entries.digest: Poitiers writes that a comet, the star kings dread, blazed soon after Harold's elevation and foretold his ruin. Writing after Hastings, he reads the spring sign through the autumn's outcome. He gives no date or position.
entries.source_note: Gesta Guillelmi, as summarised in Lewis & Portegies Zwart 2025

entries.date_display: soon after the comet's week, May 1066
entries.place: Isle of Wight and the south coast
entries.headline: Tostig sails in from overseas and raids to Sandwich
entries.digest: Straight after the comet, the Chronicle reports Earl Tostig arriving from overseas at the Isle of Wight, taking money and provisions, and harrying along the coast to Sandwich. Harold gathers a larger fleet and army than any king before him had raised. In the Chronicle's sequence, the trouble follows the sign.
entries.source_note: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle s.a. 1066, Ingram tr.

entries.headline: A white comet ten cubits long before dawn
entries.digest: Ibn al-Athir records a white comet seen just before dawn, which looked about ten cubits long and one cubit wide. It was visible until the middle of Rajab and then faded. In mid-May the real comet stood in the evening sky, so the month or the dawn timing has probably been garbled in transmission.
entries.source_note: al-Kamil s.a. 458, as quoted in Aramco World 1986

entries.headline: The comet reaches Zhang and vanishes
entries.digest: The annals record that the comet reached the lodge Zhang, in Hydra, and disappeared. The treatise sums up the apparition: star, vapour and bushiness vanished after 67 days in all. By then the comet was more than 1.5 astronomical units away and very faint, so the Kaifeng observers were watching it to the edge of visibility.
entries.source_note: Song shi annals and treatise via Yau, ch. 3 (Yau also gives 6 June for the last sighting)

entries.headline: The comet fades by the middle of Rajab
entries.digest: Ibn al-Athir's notice ends with the comet fading around the middle of Rajab. Converted, that falls within a week of the Chinese last sighting. On its end date at least, the later Arabic compilation agrees with the Song record.
entries.source_note: al-Kamil s.a. 458, as quoted in Aramco World 1986

entries.headline: A year of kings' deaths and a great nut crop
entries.digest: The Annals of Ulster's 1066 entry records Áed ua Ruairc, king of Uí Briúin, dying straight after plundering St Patrick's shrine, several killings and deaths in penitence, and a nut harvest across Ireland heavy enough to block the rivers. It does not mention the star. The Four Masters, compiling later, added it.
entries.source_note: Annals of Ulster U1066.0–4 (CELT T100001A)

entries.headline: Provisions gone, Harold sends his levies home
entries.digest: After a summer watching the coast, the Chronicle (C) says, the army's provisions ran out and the men were allowed home around the Nativity of St Mary. The king's ships moved to London and some were lost on the way. The south coast was left unguarded for the coming weeks.
entries.source_note: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle C s.a. 1066; date recalled from standard editions, not checked in the Gutenberg text

entries.headline: Harold surprises the Norwegians at Stamford Bridge
entries.digest: Harald of Norway and Tostig had landed in the north with a great fleet and beaten the northern earls near York. Harold marched north and came on them beyond York at Stamford Bridge. Both Harald and Tostig were killed, and the surviving Norwegians were allowed to sail home.
entries.source_note: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle s.a. 1066 (C, D), Ingram tr.; date as standard

entries.date_display: eve of St Michael's Mass, Thursday 28 September 1066
entries.headline: William lands at Pevensey on Michaelmas eve
entries.digest: Three days after Stamford Bridge, the Chronicle records, Count William came from Normandy into Pevensey on the eve of St Michael's Mass and built a castle at Hastings. The news reached Harold in the north. He turned south.
entries.source_note: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle s.a. 1066 (D), Ingram tr.

entries.headline: Battle on Pope Calixtus' day; Harold falls
entries.digest: The D chronicler records that Harold met William before all his army had gathered, at the grey apple tree, and that the king fell with his brothers Gyrth and Leofwine. The Frenchmen held the field. The scribe adds that God granted it to them for the people's sins.
entries.source_note: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle D s.a. 1066, Ingram tr.

entries.headline: The duke's chaplain narrates the day-long fight
entries.digest: Poitiers gives the fullest Norman account of the battle: the English shield-wall on the ridge, the feigned retreats, the duke unhorsed and remounted. Harold's death comes late in the day. He presents it as divine judgment on the perjurer the comet had warned against.
entries.source_note: Gesta Guillelmi II, as summarised in standard overviews; edition not checked directly

entries.headline: A brief Norman verdict on Hastings
entries.digest: William of Jumièges' account of the battle is short. Harold, he says, fell in the first assault, the English fled at nightfall, and the duke's victory was God's judgment. His brevity contrasts with Poitiers' long set-piece.
entries.source_note: Gesta Normannorum Ducum VII, standard summary; edition not checked directly

entries.headline: HIC HAROLD REX INTERFECTUS EST
entries.digest: The final surviving scenes show the shield-wall, Odo rallying the young men with his club, and the inscription 'here King Harold was killed' over a figure struck in the eye and a figure cut down by a horseman. Whether one or both figures are Harold has long been debated. The end of the hanging is lost.
entries.source_note: Bayeux Tapestry final scenes

entries.headline: Archbishop Ealdred hallows William king
entries.digest: On midwinter's day Archbishop Ealdred crowned William at Westminster after the king swore to rule well. The Chronicle then notes the heavy taxes that followed. The year that opened with one coronation at Westminster closes with another.
entries.quote: hallowed him to king at Westminster
entries.source_note: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle D s.a. 1066, Ingram tr.

entries.headline: Acclamation, alarm and fire at the coronation
entries.digest: Poitiers describes the shouted acclamation in Westminster Abbey. The Norman guards outside mistook it for an attack and set fire to nearby houses, and the congregation fled while the rite went on. He presents this as a sad accident at a just king's crowning.
entries.source_note: Gesta Guillelmi II, standard summary (also in Orderic Vitalis); edition not checked directly

entries.headline: Sixty years on, the old monk's cry is written down
entries.digest: William of Malmesbury sets Eilmer's outburst among the signs of 1066 in his Deeds of the English Kings. In the same work he records Eilmer's youthful attempt to fly from the abbey tower. That is how a monk who left no writing came to be the best-known English witness of the comet.
entries.source_note: Gesta Regum Anglorum (completed c. 1125); Lewis & Portegies Zwart 2025

convergences.label: Twelfth Day: Edward buried, Harold crowned
convergences.note: The English annal records a lawful hallowing. Poitiers calls it a perjurer's seizure. The Tapestry, months before the comet's real appearance, puts the star in the very next scene.

convergences.label: First dawn sightings in the east
convergences.note: Kyoto saw it first by local time, then Kaifeng, both about seven degrees of tail before sunrise. About a week later Baghdad describes a tail reaching the zenith. No European record mentions the dawn phase.

convergences.label: Lost in the glare, and a puzzling Korean star
convergences.note: In mid-April the comet passed near the Sun. Japan and Edessa describe it vanishing and returning in the west, while the Goryeo record puts a moon-sized star in the north-west on 19 April, earlier than anyone else's reappearance.

convergences.label: The evening return: eve of the Greater Litany
convergences.note: Ordered west to east by local evening: Ireland logs 25 April, England 24 April with seven nights of shining, and Kyiv a seven-day star with blood-red rays (in a misdated entry). Kaifeng, earliest by the clock, records a white vapour and puts the comet in the Pleiades.

convergences.label: Tail at its longest
convergences.note: Kaifeng measures fifteen degrees. A Norman monk sees a three-forked tail sweeping south from the north-west. Kyoto sees it in the west at dusk the next evening. The measurement and the descriptions fit the same tail.

convergences.label: Reading the sign
convergences.note: The same object was read as a scourge of England, as bloodshed for Rus', as a sign of a troubled Byzantine reign, as an Armenian omen of invasion, and as a sign of a usurper's doom. Most of these readings were written down after the events they claim it foretold.

convergences.label: Fading out
convergences.note: Kaifeng follows the comet to the lodge Zhang and its 67th day. Ibn al-Athir's later notice ends at mid-Rajab, within a week of the Chinese date.

convergences.label: Hastings
convergences.note: The English scribe blames the people's sins, Poitiers gives a long account of divine justice, and Jumièges a brief verdict. The Tapestry shows Harold's death under its famous caption. Only the Normans link the battle back to the spring star.

ties.note: William of Poitiers drew on William of Jumièges' Gesta for Norman background, and the two are the main ducal-side narratives of 1066.
The Tapestry and the Gesta Guillelmi tell closely parallel stories of Harold's oath and fall, both from Duke William's circle (the Tapestry via Bishop Odo).

The English annal names Ealdred as William's consecrator and calls Harold king without reproach; the Tapestry, made under Norman patronage, shows Stigand at Harold's crowning, a detail that cast doubt on its legitimacy.
The two nearest-contemporary western records of the comet sit on opposite shores of the Channel; one dates it exactly, the other describes its shape.
Malmesbury and Abingdon are about 50 km apart; the Abingdon scribe dated the comet while the Malmesbury monk, as later reported, prophesied over it.
Kaifeng and Kyoto both record a seven-degree broom star in the east on the morning of 3 April, the earliest dated sightings of the apparition.
The Song and Goryeo courts used the same astronomical vocabulary, but the Korean date and direction disagree with the Chinese; modern analysts leave the discrepancy unresolved.
Ibn al-Athir used Ibn al-Jawzi's al-Muntazam among his sources for Baghdad events; their comet notices differ in month and timing.
The Kyiv chronicle's 1066 entry blames a Byzantine official from Chersonesos for poisoning Prince Rostislav, during the reign Zonaras uses to date the comet.
Matthew of Edessa was often bitter about Byzantine rule over Armenians, which colours his account of these years; the two chroniclers recorded the same comet from opposite sides of that relationship.
The Irish date (Tuesday 25 April) and the English (Monday 24 April) are one night apart, each reckoned by both the Roman calendar and the Easter cycle.
The three-forked tail seen from Normandy and the fifteen-degree tail measured at Kaifeng are the same structure, seen from opposite ends of Eurasia within days.

threads_out.note: Twelve years earlier the same Song astronomical bureau, along with Japanese court observers, logged the guest star of 1054 in Taurus. The 1066 comet passed through Taurus too, near the Pleiades and Hyades, in late April.

It is the same comet, eleven returns later. By 1910 popular astronomy books, such as Chambers' Story of the Comets (1909), reproduced the Bayeux Tapestry comet and the Song records to show readers what earlier generations had seen.

Edmond Halley, whose 1715 eclipse map is the subject of that chapter, had already shown in 1705 that the comets of 1531, 1607 and 1682 were one object and predicted its return. That is how the comet of 1066 came to carry his name.

vantage_key: 0 = principal actor (none here); 1 = professional or court observers on the spot, or a writer inside the ducal circle; 2 = contemporary local annalists and witnesses; 3 = writers at a distance in place or time; 4 = a compiler working from others' notices more than a century later.

claims.claim: Broom star at dawn in the lodge Yingshi, tail c. 7° pointing SW towards Wei; first dated sighting of the apparition.
claims.evidence: Song shi astronomical treatise and annals (via Yau, ch. 3)

claims.claim: Broom star in the east, about 7° long, before dawn at Kyoto.
claims.evidence: Composite Japanese record in Kanda, via Yau

claims.claim: Large comet over Baghdad with a long tail reaching the zenith; later reappears at sunset, tail south, about 10 days.
claims.evidence: al-Muntazam, as quoted in Aramco World 1986; Hijri year inferred

claims.claim: Star in the NW as large as the Moon, turning into a bushy comet; date and direction disagree with China and Japan.

claims.date_display: VIII Kal. Mai., eve of the Greater Litany (24 April 1066)
claims.claim: Seen 'over all England'; called a comet or 'long-haired star'; first appeared 24 April and shone seven nights.
claims.evidence: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle C and D s.a. 1066

claims.claim: White vapour (the tail) reappears; comet in Mao (Pleiades), 'like Venus', 15° long; Liao court logs a broom star in the west the same day.
claims.evidence: Song shi treatise and annals; Liao shi (via Yau)

claims.claim: Tail more than 10° long and more than 3° wide; comet emerges in Bi (Hyades).
claims.evidence: Song shi treatise and annals (via Yau)

claims.date_display: VII Kal. Mai., Tuesday after Little Easter (25 April 1066)
claims.claim: A star appeared; dated by both Roman calendar and Easter cycle.
claims.evidence: Annals of the Four Masters M1066.11

claims.claim: Very large star in the west with blood-red rays, rising in the evening after sunset, seen seven days; read as a sign of feuds and pagan raids.
Comet as bright as the full moon, at first tailless; a tail grew as the head seemed to shrink.
An omen of England's ruin and of mothers' tears; Eilmer says he had seen it before (often linked to the 989 return).
claims.evidence: William of Malmesbury, Gesta Regum Anglorum II.225

claims.claim: Tail 15° long; Yau's fit of the April positions puts perihelion at c. 23.5 March, about 2.5 days after the tabulated 20.9 March.
Star in the NW with a three-forked tail stretching far into the southern sky, visible about 15 days; 'a change in some kingdom'.
White comet before dawn, about 10 cubits long and 1 cubit wide, visible until mid-Rajab; the dawn timing conflicts with the comet's evening position in May.
Comet reaches the lodge Zhang and disappears; 67 days in all.
claims.evidence: Song shi annals and treatise (via Yau)

claims.date_display: c. 1070–77 (Tapestry probably made for Bayeux Cathedral's consecration, 14 July 1077)
claims.claim: ISTI MIRANT STELLA: the comet is placed just after Harold's January coronation, though it appeared in late April, reading the star as a verdict on Harold.
claims.evidence: Bayeux Tapestry scene 32; Lewis & Portegies Zwart 2025
